title: Comparing
description: Compare people and things with plus, moins, aussi, meilleur and mieux, and say the most or the least.

guide.summary: Comparisons say that one side is more, less or as much as another; superlatives say which one is the most or the least of a group.

sections.title: Comparing a quality: plus, moins, aussi
sections.text: Put plus, moins or aussi before the adjective and que after it. The adjective still agrees with the person or thing it describes.

rows: Marie est plus grande que Paul.
Ce film est moins long que le livre.
Tu es aussi rapide que moi.

steps: Check what follows the blank: a quality of someone or something is an adjective.
Put plus, moins or aussi immediately before it, with no de.
Agree the adjective with the first person or thing named.
Close the comparison with que and the other side.

examples.fr: Marie est plus grande que son frère.
examples.en: Marie is taller than her brother.

examples.fr: Ma maison est moins petite que la tienne.
examples.en: My house is less small than yours.

watch: No de before an adjective: plus rapide que, never plus de rapide.
Autant never goes before an adjective; aussi does.
Agreement does not stop in a comparison: plus petite with a feminine noun.

sections.title: Comparing a quantity of a noun
sections.text: Before a noun, the comparison word needs de, and that de never turns into du, de la or des.

rows: J’ai plus de livres que toi.
Nous avons moins de temps que vous.
Il boit autant de café que moi.

steps: Look at what follows: a noun means you are comparing a quantity.
Take plus de, moins de or autant de and put it in front of the noun.
Keep de bare — never du, de la or des — and drop the article of the noun.
Write d’ before a vowel or a silent h: plus d’habitants.

examples.fr: Paris a plus d’habitants que Lyon.
examples.en: Paris has more inhabitants than Lyon.

examples.fr: Paul a autant de chats que Marc.
examples.en: Paul has as many cats as Marc.

watch: Aussi belongs with adjectives; an equal quantity of a noun takes autant de.
The noun loses its own article: plus de livres, not plus des livres.

sections.title: Comparing an action
sections.text: When you compare how much someone does something, the comparison word comes straight after the verb, with no de.

rows: Tu dors autant que ton frère.

steps: Ask what is compared: if no noun and no adjective follows, it is the action itself.
Use plus, moins or autant with nothing between the verb and it.
For an equal amount after a verb, use autant, not aussi.
Add que and the other side; que becomes qu’ before a vowel.

examples.en: We eat as much as you.

watch: No de after a verb: il mange plus que moi, never plus de moi.
De only appears when a noun follows: il mange plus de gâteau que moi.

sections.title: Which pronoun after que?
sections.text: After que, French uses the stressed pronoun — the same form you use after avec or pour.
steps: Find the person on the other side of the comparison.
Take that person’s stressed form from the table.
Elide que before a vowel: qu’elle, qu’eux, qu’avant.

examples.fr: Elle est plus patiente que lui.
examples.en: She is more patient than him.

watch: Never que je, que tu or que il after a comparison.

sections.title: Better: meilleur or mieux?
sections.text: Bon and bien have their own comparatives. Plus bon and plus bien simply do not exist.

rows: a noun — it agrees like an adjective

steps: Ask what better describes: a noun (a thing, a person) or a verb (how it is done).
For a noun, take the adjective form and agree it in gender and number.
For a verb, take the invariable form and leave it alone.
In a superlative, add the article: le meilleur, la meilleure, le mieux.

examples.fr: C’est le meilleur restaurant du quartier.
examples.en: It’s the best restaurant in the area.

watch: Only plus bon and plus bien are banned: moins bon, aussi bon, moins bien and aussi bien are all correct.
Never plus meilleur or plus mieux: the comparison is already inside the word.

sections.title: The most, the least
sections.text: A superlative is le, la or les + plus or moins + adjective. The group it stands out in follows with de.

rows: le plus grand élève de la classe
les plus beaux jours de l’année
le meilleur, la meilleure, les meilleures
de la classe, du quartier, de l’année

steps: Find the noun or person: its gender and number decide le, la or les.
Add plus or moins, then the adjective, agreed with that noun.
Name the group with de, never with que or à.
For bon, drop plus and use the special form after the article.

examples.fr: Emma est la plus jeune de la famille.
examples.en: Emma is the youngest in the family.

examples.fr: Elle est la moins fatiguée du groupe.
examples.en: She is the least tired in the group.

watch: De + le becomes du and de + les becomes des: du groupe, des élèves.
Never le plus bon or la plus bonne.
English “in the class” is de la classe here, not dans la classe.

sections.title: Where does the adjective go in a superlative?
sections.text: An adjective keeps its usual place. When it follows the noun, the article is repeated before plus or moins.

rows: most of them: intéressant, cher, difficile, calme, sérieux
short common ones: grand, petit, beau, jeune, bon
la plus belle ville, or la ville la plus belle

steps: Ask where the adjective sits in a plain phrase: un film intéressant, une belle ville.
If it follows the noun, keep it there and repeat the article before plus or moins.
If it goes before the noun, either order is correct.
Make both articles agree with the noun: le, la or les.

examples.fr: C’est le restaurant le moins cher de Paris.
examples.en: It’s the cheapest restaurant in Paris.

examples.fr: J’ai acheté la robe la plus chère.
examples.en: I bought the most expensive dress.

watch: The repeated article goes before plus or moins, not after it.
Never squeeze plus between the article and the noun: le plus film intéressant is wrong.

steps: Check that what follows is an adjective, not a noun and not a verb.
Place plus, moins or aussi right before the adjective, with no de.
Agree the adjective with the first person or thing, then close with que.
Look for a noun after the blank: that calls for the quantity form.
Add de after plus, moins or autant, and keep it bare — never du, de la or des.
Write d’ before a vowel or a silent h.
Check whether the comparison sits on the verb: no noun and no adjective follows it.
Use plus, moins or autant with nothing between the verb and que.
After que, take the stressed pronoun and elide to qu’ before a vowel.
Decide what better describes: a noun, or the way a verb is done.
For a noun, take the adjective form and agree it; for a verb, take the invariable one.
Never put plus in front of bon or bien.
Find the noun: its gender and number set le, la or les.
Put plus or moins after the article, with the adjective agreed.
Introduce the group with de, merging de + le into du.
For bon, use its special form after the article instead of plus.
Ask where the adjective normally sits: before or after the noun.
If it follows the noun, repeat the article before plus or moins.
If it goes before the noun, both orders are allowed.
Make every article agree with the noun.

exercises.source: Marie est plus ____ que son frère.

mistakes.why: Grand is the masculine form. The adjective agrees with Marie, and the comparison word in front of it changes nothing.
Grands is masculine plural. Only one person is described here, and she is a woman.

exercises.feedback: The adjective still agrees in a comparison.
exercises.explanation: The adjective agrees with Marie, the first person: plus grande.

exercises.source: Le train est ____ rapide que le bus.

mistakes.why: That extra de belongs in front of a noun (de livres, de temps). Rapide is an adjective, so no de is needed.
Autant compares quantities or actions, and it makes the two sides equal. Here a quality is compared, and the two sides are not equal.

exercises.feedback: With an adjective, there is no de.
exercises.explanation: Before an adjective, more is plus: plus rapide que.

exercises.instruction: Write the word for as (as … as).
exercises.source: Ma sœur est ____ sportive que moi.

mistakes.why: Autant compares quantities or actions (il mange autant que moi). Sportive is an adjective, so it takes the word French uses before adjectives.
Plus makes one side greater. The sentence puts the two sisters on the same level.
Si + adjective works in exclamations (elle est si sportive !), not in a comparison with que.

exercises.feedback: With an adjective, as … as is not autant.
exercises.explanation: Before an adjective, as … as is aussi … que: aussi sportive que moi.

exercises.source: Ce film est ____ intéressant que le livre.

mistakes.why: That extra de introduces a noun (de temps, de livres). Intéressant is an adjective, so nothing comes between.
Plus goes the other way: it would make the film more interesting than the book.
Aussi puts the two on the same level, but the sentence ranks the film below the book.

exercises.hint: You need the opposite of plus.
exercises.feedback: There is no de before an adjective.
exercises.explanation: Before an adjective, less is moins: moins intéressant que.

exercises.source: Paul is taller than Marie.
answers: Paul est plus grand que Marie.
Paul est plus grande que Marie.
mistakes.why: Paul is a man, so the adjective takes no extra e. It agrees with the person described, not with the person he is compared to.

answers: Paul est plus grand de Marie.
mistakes.why: De never means than in a comparison; it appears only before a noun of quantity or after a superlative.

answers: Paul est plus haut que Marie.
mistakes.why: Haut describes objects, walls and buildings. A person’s height uses another adjective.

exercises.feedback: Use the pattern plus + adjective + que.
exercises.explanation: Taller than is plus grand que, with grand agreeing with Paul.

exercises.instruction: Join the two sentences with aussi … que.
exercises.source: Léa est grande. Sa mère est grande aussi.
answers: Léa est aussi grande que sa mère.
Sa mère est aussi grande que Léa.
Léa est aussi grande comme sa mère.
mistakes.why: Comme is for likeness (grande comme toi). The as … as frame is closed with que.

answers: Léa est autant grande que sa mère.
mistakes.why: Autant compares quantities and actions; it is never placed before an adjective.

answers: Léa est aussi grand que sa mère.
mistakes.why: Grand here is masculine. Léa is a woman, so the adjective needs its feminine form even inside a comparison.

answers: Léa est plus grande que sa mère.
mistakes.why: Plus says one is taller than the other. The two sentences say they reach the same height.

exercises.feedback: Put the comparison word before the adjective and que after it.
exercises.explanation: Equal qualities take aussi + adjective + que: aussi grande que sa mère.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: She is more patient than him. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.source: She is more patient than him.
answers: Elle est plus patiente que lui.
Elle est plus patiente que il.
mistakes.why: Il is the subject form. After que, French uses the stressed pronoun, the one you also use after avec or pour.

answers: Elle est patiente plus que lui.
mistakes.why: The comparison word goes right before the adjective, not after it.
Without que the two sides are not joined; a comparison always needs the word that introduces what you compare to.

exercises.hint: After que, use a stressed pronoun.
exercises.feedback: Check the pronoun after que.
exercises.explanation: The pattern is plus + adjective + que, and after que the pronoun is lui, not il.

exercises.source: Ma maison est plus petit que ta maison.
answers: Ma maison est plus petite que ta maison.
Ma maison est plus petit que ta maison.
mistakes.why: This leaves the adjective in its masculine form. Maison is feminine, so the adjective has to agree even inside a comparison.

answers: Ma maison est plus petite de ta maison.
mistakes.why: De never means than. It appears only before a noun of quantity or after a superlative.

answers: Ma maison est moins petite que ta maison.
mistakes.why: Moins reverses the meaning. Only the ending of the adjective was wrong in the original sentence.

exercises.feedback: The adjective still has to agree.
exercises.explanation: Petite agrees with the feminine noun maison, even in a comparison.

exercises.source: J’ai ____ livres que toi.

mistakes.why: Alone, the word compares actions (il travaille beaucoup). Livres is a noun, so the quantity form is needed.
Des is an article. In this frame de stays bare in front of the noun and never merges with an article.

exercises.feedback: Before a noun, you need a small extra word.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, more is plus de, and de does not change: plus de livres.

exercises.source: Il boit ____ café que moi.

mistakes.why: Aussi goes before an adjective (aussi fort que toi). Café is a noun, so it needs the quantity form.
Du is de + le, an article. Before the noun here, de stays bare and never combines with an article.

exercises.feedback: Aussi goes with adjectives, not nouns.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, as much is autant de: autant de café.

exercises.source: Nous avons ____ temps que vous.

mistakes.why: On its own the word compares actions (je sors moins qu’avant). Temps is a noun, so one small word is still missing.
Du and de la are articles. In this frame de stays bare in front of the noun.
Que introduces what you compare to, and it already stands later in the sentence. What is missing before temps is the quantity word.
Peu de means little in itself; it states an amount instead of comparing two of them.

exercises.feedback: Before a noun you need two words.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, less is moins de: moins de temps.

exercises.instruction: Write the words for as many.
exercises.source: Elle a ____ cousins que sa sœur.

mistakes.why: Aussi goes before an adjective. Cousins is a noun, so the word for an equal quantity is a different one.
On its own, the word goes after a verb (elle travaille autant que sa sœur), and des is an article. In front of a noun the quantity word needs its bare partner.
Même means same and describes the noun itself; it cannot be paired with que to compare two amounts.

exercises.feedback: Aussi does not go with nouns.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, as many is autant de: autant de cousins.

exercises.source: I have more work than you (to a friend).
answers: J’ai plus de travail que toi.
J’ai davantage de travail que toi.
J’ai plus de travail que tu.
mistakes.why: Tu is the subject form. After que, French uses the stressed pronoun, the one you also use after avec.
In front of a noun the quantity word needs its small partner; without it, travail is left hanging.

answers: Je ai plus de travail que toi.
mistakes.why: Je becomes j’ before a vowel; je ai is never written.

answers: J’ai plus de travail que vous.
mistakes.why: Vous is the polite or plural form. The sentence says you are speaking to a friend.

exercises.feedback: Check the word after plus and the pronoun after que.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, more is plus de, and after que the pronoun is toi: plus de travail que toi.

exercises.source: Tom has fewer brothers than Julie.
answers: Tom a moins de frères que Julie.
Tom a moins frères que Julie.
mistakes.why: Before a noun the quantity word needs its small partner; without it, frères is left hanging.

answers: Tom a moins des frères que Julie.
mistakes.why: Des is an article. The quantity word keeps de bare and the noun loses its own article.

answers: Tom a moins de frères comme Julie.
mistakes.why: Comme is for likeness. A comparison of quantities is closed with que.

answers: Tom a peu de frères que Julie.
mistakes.why: Peu de means few in itself and cannot be paired with que; the sentence compares two people.

exercises.feedback: Before a noun, add a small word after moins.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, fewer is moins de: moins de frères.

exercises.source: Paris a plus des habitants que Lyon.
answers: Paris a plus d’habitants que Lyon.
Paris a plus des habitants que Lyon.
mistakes.why: Des is an article. After the quantity word, de stays bare and the noun loses its article.

answers: Paris a plus de habitants que Lyon.
mistakes.why: De loses its e in front of a vowel or a silent h; de habitants is never written.

answers: Paris a plus habitants que Lyon.
mistakes.why: Dropping the small word leaves the noun with nothing to link it to the quantity word.

exercises.hint: After plus, the small word never changes to des.
exercises.feedback: Look at the word after plus, and remember elision.
exercises.explanation: The pattern is plus de + noun, and de becomes d’ before a vowel or silent h: plus d’habitants.

exercises.instruction: Join the two sentences with autant de … que.
exercises.source: Paul a trois chats. Marc a trois chats aussi.
answers: Paul a autant de chats que Marc.
Marc a autant de chats que Paul.
Paul a aussi de chats que Marc.
mistakes.why: Aussi belongs before an adjective, never in front of a noun.

answers: Paul a autant chats que Marc.
mistakes.why: In front of a noun the quantity word needs its small partner; without it, chats is left hanging.

answers: Paul a autant des chats que Marc.
mistakes.why: Des is an article. The quantity word keeps de bare and the noun loses its own article.

exercises.feedback: Use the pattern for equal quantities of a noun.
exercises.explanation: Equal quantities of a noun take autant de + noun + que: autant de chats que Marc.

exercises.source: Il travaille ____ que moi.

mistakes.why: That extra de introduces a noun (de travail, de temps). Here the comparison sits on the verb travaille, so nothing comes between it and que.
Bien is never compared by putting a word in front of it, and the sentence compares how much he works, not how well.

exercises.hint: You are comparing an action, not a thing.
exercises.feedback: After a verb, no de is needed.
exercises.explanation: After a verb, more is simply plus: il travaille plus que moi.

exercises.source: Tu dors ____ que ton frère.

mistakes.why: Aussi goes before an adjective (aussi fatigué que toi). Dors is a verb, so the equal-amount word is a different one.
De is added only when a noun follows (de café, de sommeil). Here que comes straight after.

exercises.feedback: Aussi goes with adjectives; after a verb, as much is different.
exercises.explanation: After a verb, as much is autant: tu dors autant que ton frère.

exercises.source: Je sors ____ qu’avant.

mistakes.why: De is added only before a noun (de sorties). Here the comparison sits on the verb sors.
Plus says the opposite: that you go out more than before.
Aussi goes before an adjective, and it makes two sides equal; here the action has gone down.
Mieux is the comparative of bien: it says how well something is done, not how much.

exercises.feedback: After a verb, no de is needed.
exercises.explanation: After a verb, less is moins: je sors moins qu’avant.

exercises.source: She reads more than me.

mistakes.why: De never means than. It appears only before a noun of quantity or after a superlative.
Je is the subject form. After que, French uses the stressed pronoun, the one you also use after avec.
Mieux says how well she reads. The English compares how much she reads.

exercises.feedback: Check the word after the verb and the pronoun after que.
exercises.explanation: After a verb, more is plus, and after que the pronoun is moi: elle lit plus que moi.

exercises.source: We eat as much as you (you, plural).

mistakes.why: Aussi is for adjectives; after a verb it cannot carry the meaning as much.
Toi addresses one friend. The English says you in the plural.
Manger keeps its e before the -ons ending, to keep the soft g sound.

exercises.feedback: After a verb, as much is not aussi.
exercises.explanation: After a verb, as much as is autant que: nous mangeons autant que vous.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: He works less than her. Leave the extra tiles unused.
exercises.source: He works less than her.

mistakes.why: De belongs only before a noun. Nothing is counted here, so nothing comes between the comparison word and que.
The comparison word follows the verb; it does not come in front of it.

exercises.hint: After a verb, no de is needed.
exercises.feedback: Check the words after moins.
exercises.explanation: After a verb, less than is moins que, and que becomes qu’ before elle.

exercises.source: Mon frère mange plus de moi.
answers: Mon frère mange plus que moi.
Mon frère mange plus de moi.
mistakes.why: Left as it is, the sentence puts de in front of a person. De introduces a noun of quantity, not the other side of a comparison.

answers: Mon frère mange plus que je.
mistakes.why: Je is the subject form. After que, French uses the stressed pronoun, the one you also use after avec.

answers: Mon frère mange autant que moi.
mistakes.why: Autant makes the two equal, but the sentence says one eats more than the other.

exercises.hint: Moi is a person, not a quantity.
exercises.feedback: The word before moi is wrong.
exercises.explanation: After a verb, the comparison is plus que: il mange plus que moi. De is only for a noun after plus.

exercises.source: Ce gâteau est ____ que l’autre.

mistakes.why: Bon is never compared by putting a word in front of it; it changes into a special form instead.
This is the feminine form, with an extra e. Gâteau is masculine (un gâteau), so it cannot agree that way.

exercises.hint: Better here describes gâteau, a masculine noun.
exercises.feedback: Bon has a special comparative form.
exercises.explanation: Better describing a masculine noun is meilleur: ce gâteau est meilleur.

exercises.source: Elle chante ____ que moi.

mistakes.why: Meilleur is an adjective: it describes a noun (un meilleur chanteur). Here the word describes how she sings, which is a verb.
Bien never takes a word in front of it to be compared; it has its own single-word form.

exercises.hint: Better here describes how she sings.
exercises.feedback: Bien has a special comparative form.
exercises.explanation: Better describing a verb is mieux: elle chante mieux que moi.

exercises.source: C’est une ____ idée.

mistakes.why: This is the masculine form. Idée is feminine (une idée), so an ending is missing.
Mieux replaces bien and goes with a verb. Idée is a noun, so it takes an adjective that agrees with it.

exercises.hint: Better here describes idée, a feminine noun.
exercises.feedback: This word agrees like an adjective.
exercises.explanation: Better describing a noun is meilleur, and it agrees with the feminine idée: une meilleure idée.

exercises.instruction: Write meilleur or mieux, in the right form.
exercises.source: Tu nages ____ que l’année dernière.

mistakes.why: Meilleur and its endings are adjective forms, used with a noun (un meilleur nageur). Nages is a verb, so the word must not agree at all.
Bien is never compared by putting a word in front of it; it has its own single-word form.
Bien alone says that you swim well, but it does not compare this year with last year.

exercises.hint: Better here describes how you swim.
exercises.feedback: This describes an action, not a thing.
exercises.explanation: Better describing a verb is mieux, which never changes: tu nages mieux.

exercises.instruction: Write meilleur or mieux, in the right form.
exercises.source: Ces pommes sont ____ que les autres.

mistakes.why: This is the masculine singular form. Pommes is feminine and plural, so two marks are missing.
This agrees as feminine but stays singular. Pommes is plural, so one letter is still missing.
This is the masculine plural. Une pomme is feminine, so the feminine plural is the one needed.
Mieux goes with a verb and never changes. Here the word describes pommes, a noun.
Bon is never compared by putting a word in front of it; it has its own form, which agrees like any adjective.

exercises.hint: Better here describes pommes, a feminine plural noun.
exercises.feedback: This word agrees like an adjective.
exercises.explanation: Better describing a noun is meilleur, and it agrees with pommes: meilleures.

exercises.source: Ce restaurant est plus bon que l’autre.
answers: Ce restaurant est meilleur que l’autre.
Ce restaurant est plus bon que l’autre.
mistakes.why: Bon never takes a comparison word in front of it; it changes shape instead.

answers: Ce restaurant est mieux que l’autre.
mistakes.why: Mieux replaces bien and goes with a verb (il mange mieux). Here the word describes restaurant, a noun.

answers: Ce restaurant est meilleure que l’autre.
mistakes.why: Restaurant is masculine (un restaurant), so this feminine ending does not agree with it.

answers: Ce restaurant est plus meilleur que l’autre.
mistakes.why: The special form already means more good; a second comparison word doubles it.

exercises.feedback: Bon has a special comparative form.
exercises.explanation: The comparative of bon is meilleur: ce restaurant est meilleur que l’autre.

exercises.source: Il joue plus bien que son père.
answers: Il joue mieux que son père.
Il joue plus bien que son père.
mistakes.why: Bien is never compared by putting a word in front of it; it has its own single-word form.

answers: Il joue meilleur que son père.
mistakes.why: Meilleur is an adjective describing a noun (un meilleur joueur). Joue is a verb.

answers: Il joue plus mieux que son père.
mistakes.why: The one-word comparative already means more well; a second comparison word doubles it.

exercises.feedback: Bien has a special comparative form.
exercises.explanation: The comparative of bien is mieux: il joue mieux que son père.

exercises.source: My sister cooks better than me.
answers: Ma sœur cuisine mieux que moi.
Ma sœur fait mieux la cuisine que moi.
Ma sœur cuisine meilleur que moi.
Ma sœur cuisine meilleure que moi.
mistakes.why: Meilleur is an adjective for a noun (une meilleure cuisinière). Cuisine here is a verb: it says what she does.

answers: Ma sœur cuisine mieux que je.
mistakes.why: Je is the subject form. After que, French uses the stressed pronoun, the one you also use after avec.

answers: Ma sœur cuisine plus bien que moi.
mistakes.why: Bien is never compared by putting a word in front of it; it has its own single-word form.

exercises.feedback: This describes an action, and check the pronoun after que.
exercises.explanation: Better describing a verb is mieux, and after que the pronoun is moi.

exercises.source: C’est le plus grand élève ____ la classe.

mistakes.why: Que introduces the other side when you compare two people or things (plus grand que Tom). A superlative names the group someone stands out in, which is introduced differently.
À marks a place you go to or a person you give something to. It does not introduce the group of a superlative.

exercises.hint: In the class is part of a superlative.
exercises.feedback: After a superlative, French does not use que or à for the group.
exercises.explanation: After a superlative, the group is introduced with de: le plus grand élève de la classe.

exercises.source: Julie est ____ plus rapide de l’équipe.

mistakes.why: Le is masculine. Julie is a woman, so the article of the superlative must be feminine.
Les is plural. Only one person is named here.

exercises.feedback: The article agrees too.
exercises.explanation: The article in a superlative agrees with the person: Julie est la plus rapide.

exercises.source: Ce sont ____ plus beaux jours de l’année.

mistakes.why: Le is masculine singular. Jours is plural, so the article has to show it.
La is feminine singular. Un jour is masculine, and there are several of them here.
Des is the plural of un and une. A superlative always takes the definite article.

exercises.feedback: The article agrees with the noun.
exercises.explanation: Jours is plural, so the superlative takes les: les plus beaux jours.

exercises.instruction: Write the words for the best.
exercises.source: C’est ____ restaurant du quartier.

mistakes.why: Bon is never compared by putting a word in front of it, and that holds in a superlative too.
Restaurant is masculine (un restaurant), so this feminine pair does not agree with it.
On its own the special form is a comparative: better than something else. The top of a group needs an article in front of it.
Mieux goes with a verb (c’est lui qui cuisine le mieux). Restaurant is a noun, so it takes the adjective form.
